sm: The Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop on Friday, halting departures at all U.S. airports because of what it called extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety. An advisory reposted by Transportation Secretary Scott Duffy said all departing traffic should remain grounded until further notice, with inbound international flights handled case by case. Officials first blamed an equipment outage. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a threat to the United States, calling it a telecommunications outage across the FAA. He said flights were grounded out of caution, all were accounted for, and airborne planes should expect landing delays.

Police say the gunman who shot up a popular Washington, D.C., neighborhood before taking his own life was a 55-year-old doctor named Matt Lambert. He killed his building manager in a gym, then barricaded himself in his apartment and wounded four more people from his balcony. Police believe he may also have tried to set the building on fire, and the interim police chief said accelerant was likely used. Lambert had been in a legal fight with building management over mold, and witnesses said he told people he did it to get attention. His attorney said he was deeply saddened and that litigation never calls for violence.

The first major post-election rift among Democrats has broken out in the Senate. Senator Chris Van Hollen launched a bid to replace Chuck Schumer as party leader, saying he would unrig an economy rigged against working people, and Bernie Sanders is backing the push. Schumer says he is confident he has the votes to stay. Fifty-four young Sunrise Movement activists were arrested after a sit-in at Schumer's office, demanding his replacement and an end to the filibuster. Separately, Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed suggested Democrats who support Israel no longer belong in the party, saying Representative Haley Stevens effectively expelled herself by endorsing his Republican opponent.

Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott is demanding testimony from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over Huang's alleged Chinese spy affair. Scott sent letters Thursday asking both men to appear voluntarily at separate public hearings, Huang on December 3 and Lutnick on December 10. He warned the committee could subpoena Huang if he refuses. Scott said recent reports raise serious national security concerns and that Americans deserve answers. The letters cite the committee's authority over export controls and its oversight of laws governing sensitive technology exports.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is urging owners of more than 720,000 BMW vehicles to park outside and away from buildings until repairs are done, because of a fire risk. BMW announced the recall after finding that an improperly sealed electrical connector on the water pump could be exposed to water and short circuit. The vehicles were recalled in 2024 for the same issue, but the agency knows of 10 fires after repairs. BMW is still developing a fix. Affected models run from 2012 through 2018, including the 3 series, 5 series, X1, X3, X4, X5 and Z4.

Microsoft says it is seeing encouraging recovery progress after a global outage that affected millions of users, though some may still have issues. The hours-long outage began around noon Eastern on Thursday and hit Outlook email access, affecting individuals, governments, health services, banks and railways. Down Detector says it reached 74 countries and territories within about an hour. Microsoft says the outage was not caused by a cybersecurity breach.

Ford is opening a massive new archive outside Detroit that brings roughly 150 historic vehicles under one roof. The 79,000 square foot Ford vault features a 1910 Model T, World War II era military vehicles, concept cars, racing machines and a ten cylinder Mustang. Archives manager Ted Ryan said the collection includes more than 60 concept vehicles and about 50 racing cars previously stored in several Michigan locations. The vault is meant to preserve the company's history and inspire future designers and engineers. Ryan said that to look forward, you always have to know where you've been.

ICE recorded the most arrests and deportations in its history during fiscal year 2026, according to new DHS data. It made roughly 491,000 arrests and carried out 483,000 deportations in the year running from October 2025 through September 2026. The deportation total topped the previous record of 442,640 set the year before. This year's arrests alone exceeded the combined total of the three full fiscal years under former President Biden, which was fewer than 427,000. Deportations this year nearly matched the roughly 486,000 recorded across fiscal years 2022 through 2024 under Biden.
